# Background {#sec-background}

## Fraud detection as supervised learning with extreme class imbalance

Fraud detection is typically cast as supervised binary classification. A model is trained on historical transactions labelled as fraudulent or legitimate, and assigns each incoming transaction a score by which transactions are ranked for investigation. What separates the task from the textbook classification setting is the extreme class distribution discussed in @sec-intro-fraud. Learning from data in which one class is rare is a long-studied problem in machine learning, because a learner optimising an ordinary objective over such data is dominated by the majority class and characterises the minority class poorly [@he2009learning_imbalanced_data].

The remedies proposed in the imbalanced-learning literature operate at two levels [@he2009learning_imbalanced_data]. Data-level methods alter the training distribution itself. The majority class is undersampled, the minority class is oversampled, or synthetic minority examples are generated, as in SMOTE, which interpolates new minority rows between neighbouring existing ones [@chawla2002smote]. Oversampling need not treat the minority class as homogeneous. Cluster-based oversampling (CBO) first clusters each class and then oversamples within the clusters, addressing within-class imbalance in tandem with the between-class imbalance [@jo2004class_imbalances_small_disjuncts; @he2009learning_imbalanced_data]. Algorithm-level methods leave the data unchanged and modify the learning objective instead. Cost-sensitive losses assign a higher misclassification cost to the minority class, and the focal loss reshapes the cross-entropy so that the many easy majority examples contribute little to the gradient and training concentrates on the hard, rare cases [@lin2017_focal_loss].

When working under extreme imbalances, these choices can matter more than the choice of model. In a study on bank account fraud, how the class distribution and the learning objective are treated affected minority-class performance more than which architecture was used [@sun2025extreme_imbalance_baf]. This ordering of concerns motivates the perspective of this thesis. The context-construction strategies studied here are data-level treatments applied at test time, since for an in-context-learning model the composition of the context window determines the class distribution the model effectively learns from.

## Evaluation under extreme imbalance {#sec-bg-eval}

As elaborated in @sec-intro-fraud, plain classification accuracy is uninformative at the fraud-level skew visualised in @fig-dataset-prevalence. The problem extends to the most widely used threshold-free metric, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). The ROC curve plots the true-positive rate against the false-positive rate (FPR), and the FPR normalises the false alarms by the total number of negatives. When legitimate transactions outnumber fraudulent ones by two or three orders of magnitude, even thousands of false alarms move the FPR only marginally, so both accuracy and ROC-AUC remain optimistically high for a detector whose alerts are dominated by false positives [@fawcett2006roc_analysis; @saito2015pr_more_informative_imbalanced].

Precision–recall analysis avoids this dilution. Precision, the fraction of alerts that are truly fraudulent, is computed over the predicted positives rather than over the vast negative class, so every false alarm counts against it. The area under the precision–recall curve (PR-AUC, estimated as average precision) also has an interpretable floor: a random scorer attains a PR-AUC equal to the fraud prevalence. Although a curve dominates in ROC space if and only if it dominates in PR space [@davis2006relationship_pr_roc], differences between detectors that appear negligible in ROC space become clearly visible in PR space under heavy imbalance, which makes PR-AUC the more informative primary metric [@saito2015pr_more_informative_imbalanced]. PR-AUC is thus used as the primary metric of this thesis.

PR-AUC summarises the entire operating range, but a deployed detector runs at a single operating point determined by its investigation capacity set by the users. As noted in @sec-intro-fraud, every alert consumes costly review resources, so usually the tolerable false-alarm rate is fixed in advance. Recall at a fixed FPR reports the share of fraud caught within exactly such a false-alarm budget [@leborgne2022fraud_detection_handbook], and it is the headline metric of the Bank Account Fraud benchmark, which reports recall at 5 % FPR [@jesus2022baf_arxiv; @sun2025extreme_imbalance_baf]. This thesis reports recall at both 1 % and 5 % FPR alongside PR-AUC.

One property shared by these metrics carries argumentative weight later in the thesis. PR-AUC, Recall@FPR and ROC-AUC are ranking metrics, thus they depend only on the ordering of the scores, and are therefore invariant to any monotone rescaling of a scorer's outputs [@fawcett2006roc_analysis; @davis2006relationship_pr_roc]. Post-hoc corrections for class imbalance, such as moving the decision threshold or rescaling a fixed scorer's outputs to a new class prior [@saerens2002adjusting_priors], are exactly such monotone transformations and consequently cannot move these metrics. Empirically, rebalancing the training data of conventional models has likewise been found to shift calibration rather than discrimination [@vandengoorbergh2022harm_imbalance_corrections]. An improvement measured on ranking metrics therefore reflects a genuinely different ranking of transactions, not a recalibration that thresholding could reproduce. This invariance is the basis of the response to the critique of @mcdowell2026correcting_imbalance_pfn, who argues that imbalance corrections for tabular foundation models amount to threshold adjustments. The experimental setting of this thesis is also considerably more involved than the one that critique examines, a point elaborated in @sec-related-work. The invariance argument is exact only when a single scoring function ranks the entire test set. The retrieval-based conditions evaluated later, which fit separate models to different parts of the test set, fall far outside it.

## Tabular machine learning and gradient-boosted trees {#sec-bg-gbdt}


Tabular data is organised into rows of observations and columns of features. The features are heterogeneous and can be both numerical and categorical. Each column carries its own meaning and distribution of values, which can vary wildly. This heterogeneity separates tabular learning from vision and language, where deep learning has long dominated. On tabular data, tree-based models have remained the state of the art [@grinsztajn2022why_tree_based]. A systematic benchmark attributes the gap to properties of the data itself. Tabular target functions are irregular rather than smooth, many features are uninformative, and the informative signal is aligned with the original feature axes, all of which favour axis-aligned trees over neural networks [@grinsztajn2022why_tree_based].

The strongest tree-based model family is gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs), introduced in @sec-intro-tfm as the long-standing standard for tabular classification. A GBDT is an ensemble of shallow decision trees built sequentially. Each new tree is fitted to the gradient of the loss with respect to the predictions of the ensemble built so far, so every iteration corrects the errors that remain from the previous ones [@friedman2001greedy_function_approximation]. The practical dominance of the family rests on three implementations, which differ mainly in engineering. XGBoost combines a regularised objective with sparsity-aware split finding and a scalable system design [@chen2016xgboost_scalable_tree_boosting]. LightGBM accelerates training with histogram-based splits and gradient-based data sampling [@ke2017lightgbm]. CatBoost adds ordered boosting and native handling of categorical features [@dorogush2018catboost]. These implementations, and ensembles built on top of them, occupy the top of tabular benchmarks and applied competitions alike [@grinsztajn2022why_tree_based].

In this thesis, GBDTs are the reference point. XGBoost and CatBoost are trained with the full training set, having no restrictions on how much of it they see. As discussed in @sec-context-waste, the comparison against the foundation models, which can only see a fraction of the data at once, is deliberately asymmetric. The limited context window is an inherent property of the models under evaluation.

## In-context learning and prior-data fitted networks {#sec-bg-pfn}

A major breakthrough in deep learning was the transformer architecture, built on self-attention [@vaswani2017attention_is_all_you_need]. Large language models built on transformers revealed a capability now called in-context learning (ICL). The model conditions on input-output examples supplied in its prompt and predicts new cases from them, without any update to its weights [@brown2020language_models_few_shot]. 

Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) were first proposed by @muller2022transformers_bayesian_inference as a novel way to approximate the posterior predictive distribution (PPD) in one forward pass. A PFN is a transformer trained on millions of small synthetic datasets drawn from a prior over different data-generating mechanisms. Training minimises the cross-entropy on held-out labels of those synthetic tasks, which approximates minimising the Kullback-Leibler divergence to the true PPD [@muller2022transformers_bayesian_inference]. 

One consequence of this construction carries through the rest of this thesis. The labelled context is the only data the approximated PPD conditions on. The model holds no memory of the target task in its weights, so the composition of the context determines the prediction [@muller2022transformers_bayesian_inference]. PFNs can thus be viewed as the bridge from the classical models of @sec-bg-gbdt to the tabular foundation models introduced next.

## Tabular foundation models {#sec-bg-tfm}

Building on top of the mechanism of prior-data fitted networks. The next step was TabPFN, presented by @hollmann2023tabpfn. It was optimised specifically for tabular data. Modifications to the attention masks shortened inference times, and the architecture was enabled to work on datasets with different numbers of features [@hollmann2023tabpfn]. With the second version of TabPFN a plethora of improvements were delivered [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model]. It scales to 50 times larger datasets, supports regression tasks, handles categorical data and missing values natively, and is robust to unimportant features and outliers. With these improvements TabPFN v2 reached the tuned GBDTs discussed in @sec-intro-tfm.

Further versions have continued to improve on the first ones. TabPFN v2.5 [@grinsztajn2025tabpfn25_arxiv], TabPFN v2.6 [@priorlabs2026tabpfn26_model_card] and TabPFN v3 [@grinsztajn2026tabpfn3_technical_report] extend the same family, and TabICLv2, whose name comes directly from the in-context learning mechanism, provided extensive performance increases as an architecture of its own [@qu2026tabiclv2]. The five tabular foundation models evaluated in this thesis come from this lineage.

The strong results have limits. A recent large benchmark finds that tabular foundation models excel on small and medium independent and identically distributed (IID) data, while tree-based models still dominate on non-IID, large and high-dimensional datasets [@purucker2026beyond_iid_tabular_foundation_models]. Fraud data violates the IID-assumption by being both grouped and temporal, so it sits in exactly the regime where a TFM may need some additional context tuning. Tabular foundation models have nevertheless already been applied in finance settings [@olusegun2024ifs_tabpfn_ethereum;@priorlabs_taktile_case_study; @tanna2026data_presentation_resampling].

## Context-window bottleneck under extreme imbalance {#sec-bg-bottleneck}

The context window of a tabular foundation model is fixed and modest for a reason. The cost of self-attention grows with the number of examples in the context [@vaswani2017attention_is_all_you_need], so the window cannot simply be enlarged until the training data fits. @sec-context-waste quantified what a randomly filled window contains under fraud-level imbalance. The mechanism of @sec-bg-pfn explains why that is so damaging. The PPD is constructed directly from the context window, so the context is the model's entire world for that prediction. There is no training-time memory of fraud to fall back on, thus the minority class must be characterised from the couple of examples that made it into the window.

The context is, however, not fixed by the model. It is a test-time input, and choosing it is an effective lever. Even adversarial work demonstrates this leverage. Small manipulations of the context change the predictions materially, and replacing context rows serves as a defence without touching the model weights [@djilani2025robustness_tabular_foundation_models]. If the composition of the context determines the prediction, the question becomes how to compose it. The following chapter will review what the literature proposes, and what it predicts for heavy class imbalance.
